documentation.range:
The Mainland Clouded Leopard is found from the Himalayan foothills in Nepal through Mainland Southeast Asia into China (Nowell and Jackson 1996). Mainland Clouded Leopard is extinct on the island of Taiwan (Chiang et al. 2015) and numbers are very low, and the species may be close to extirpation, in Viet Nam (Wilcox et al. 2014), China, and Bangladesh.

Bhutan
With a forest cover of 60%, the vast majority of the available habitat in Bhutan is suitable for the Mainland Clouded Leopard. However, due to the rapid increase in latitudinal elevation, Mainland Clouded Leopards have a much higher probability of occurring in the southern forested areas both inside and outside of protected areas than the northern forested areas (Penjor et al. 2018). Using an occupancy sampling framework, Mainland Clouded Leopard data gathered from the national tiger survey showed that the species was predicted to occur across the majority of the National Parks and connecting wildlife corridors including the Wangchuck Centennial National Park, Sakteng Wildlife Sanctuary, Jigme Dorji National Park, Bundling Wildlife Sanctuary, but with the highest probability in the southern protected areas of Royal Manas National Park (Tempa et al. 2013), Phipsoo Wildlife Sanctuary, Phrumsengla National Park, Jomotshankha Wildlife Sanctuary, Jigme Khesar Strict Nature Reserve, and Jigme Singye Wangchuck National Park (Lungten et al. unpub. data).

Nepal
Mainland Clouded Leopard were believed to be extinct in Nepal until 1987, when two cubs were captured alive by local communities in southeast Nepal (Dinerstein and Metha 1989) with the first camera-trap record, from Shivapuri Nagarjuna National Park in 2010 (Ghimirey and Acharya 2016). The expansion of camera-trapping studies across the country has subsequently demonstrated that Mainland Clouded Leopard occurs relatively extensively in eastern Nepal from the Terai in the south (e.g. Chitwan and Parsa National Park) up to the Nepal-Tibet (China) border in the north (e.g. Langtang NP) and as far west as Annapurna Conservation Area. Confirmed records for the species have been made from the protected areas of Kanchenjunga Conservation Area, Manaslu Conservation Area, Annapurna Conservation Area, Langtang National Park, Shivapuri Nagarjuna National Park, Chitwan National Park and Parsa National Park and from the districts of Khotang. Records west of Annapurna (e.g. Kailali district Ghodaghodi Lake, Api-Nampa Conservation Area) have been questioned. Annapurna remains the westerly extent of the species’ known global distribution (Ghimrey and Acharya 2016). However, recent seizure of a pelt that supposedly originated in Pyuthan district provides a possibility of pushing the westernmost limit further west by around 100 km (Ghimirey and Acharya 2018). In addition, an interview with a Nepalese park ranger produced a credible firsthand observation of a Mainland Clouded Leopard in Khaptad National Park (A. Bashyal and A. J. Giordano unpub. data). In Langtang National Park Mainland Clouded Leopards have been detected from altitudes as high as 3,498 m (Can et al. 2020).

India
Mainland Clouded Leopard occurs widely in northeastern India as far west as Valmiki Tiger Reserve in Bihar (Shafi et al. 2019) with recent records from protected areas in at least Sikkim (Bashir et al. 2011), West Bengal (Jhala et al. 2020), Assam (Borah et al. 2014), Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, and Mizoram (Mukherjee et al. 2019). Mukherjee et al. (2019) reported on camera-trap studies from 10 sites across five northeast Indian states with Mainland Clouded Leopard present from six sites. The extensive camera-trapping and surveys for the 2018 All India Tiger Census recorded Mainland Clouded Leopard from Kaziranga, Nameri and Manas Tiger Reserves, Assam; Pakke, Kamlang and Namdapha Tiger Reserves, Arunachal Pradesh, Buxa Tiger Reserve, West Bengal, and Dampa Tiger Reserve, Mizoram (Jhala et al. 2020). Published Mainland Clouded Leopard density estimates from Manas National Park (Borah et al.2014) and Dampa Tiger Reserve (Singh and MacDonald 2017) of 4.7 and 5.1 individuals per 100 km2 are amongst the highest recorded across the species’ range.

Bangladesh
Mainland Clouded Leopard likely persists in very small numbers in suitable mountainous habitat in part of the Chittagong Hill Tracts of southeast Bangladesh with at least one camera-trap photograph from Sangu-Matamuhuri Reserve Forest collected by parabiologists between 2011 and 2015 (Creative Conservation Alliance 2016).

Myanmar
The vast majority of Myanmar is ecologically suitable for, and within the historic range of, Mainland Clouded Leopard. However, as a result of hunting and habitat loss, the species is now likely very thinly but widely distributed across the dense evergreen forests particularly of northern (e.g. Kachin / Sagain) and southern Myanmar (e.g. Kayin, Taninthayi; Zaw et al. 2014, Greenspan et al. 2020). Zaw et al. (2019) reported widespread occurrence in Kachin (Hukaung Valley Wildlife Sanctuary, Hkakaborazi National Park Imaw Bum, Bumphar Bum Area, Hphonkanrazi Wildlife Sanctuary, Myit Sone Area) and Sagaing States (Htamanthi Wildlife Sanctuary, Alaungdaw Kathapa National Park Proposed Mahamying Wildlife Sanctuary, Mt. Saramati Area) in the north of the country with an apparently more reduced distribution in Rakhine (Rakhine Yoma), Bago (Bago Yoma) and Shan States (Paunglaung Area). Recent camera-trapping coordinated by the Kawthoolei Forestry Department (KFD) has recorded Mainland Clouded Leopard from a number of protected areas in Kayin State, including Kweekoh Wildlife Sanctuary, Kadoh Mae Nyaw Wildlife Sanctuary, Yoe Mu Kyo (proposed Wildlife Sanctuary), Megatha Wildlife Sanctuary, Maw Kee (proposed Wildlife Sanctuary), and various unprotected forested areas, including the newly formed Salween Peace Park (Moo et al. 2018; KFD unpub. data). However, the species has not been detected in some apparently suitable areas, such as Tu Ter Lor Wildlife Sanctuary and Klermu Thoepli Wildlife Sanctuary, and the number of individuals detected in any area was low (Moo et al. 2018, KFD unpublished data) with a patchy distribution throughout the region (Greenspan et al. 2020). Mainland Clouded Leopard appears widespread in Tanintharyi with recent records from most camera-trapping studies across the landscape, such as Tanintharyi Nature Reserve, Kaser Doh Conservation Landscape, Ler Mu Lah, and Lenya Reserve Forests (KFD unpub. data).

Lao PDR: Mainland Clouded Leopard were historically distributed throughout Lao PDR but the species has experienced significant declines prior to, and during, the assessment period driven by intensive hunting, most notably snaring. The most significant Mainland Clouded Leopard population remains in Nam Et Phou Louey NPA where the species is the most widely distributed large carnivore, although a decrease in density was detected between 2013 and 2017, suggesting its future in the park is not secured unless snaring is reduced (Rasphone 2018). In the rest of Lao PDR, Mainland Clouded Leopard has become extremely rare and is likely extirpated from many apparently suitable areas of forested habitat. For example, extensive camera-trap surveys within Nakai Nam Theun National Park since 2018 has not detected the species (which had been present in low numbers between 2007-2011, Coudrat et al. 2014; Coudrat, in litt. 2020). Mainland Clouded Leopard remains present in some Karst limestone protected areas, such as Phou Hin Poun NPA, where there has been less pressure from hunting (Brakels and Somdachit, 2020). West of the Mekong there are a couple of recent camera-trap records from Nam Poui NPA (2016/17; F. Guegan, in litt. 2020). There are no recent records from southern Lao PDR (e.g. Xe Sap NPA or Xe Pian NPA) and if Mainland Clouded Leopard persist in southern Lao PDR they likely do so in extremely low numbers.

China
The Mainland Clouded Leopard historically had a wide distribution in China, south of the Yangtze, but recent records are few, habitat is fast disappearing, illegal hunting of this species has been prolific and its current distribution in China is poorly known and appears largely restricted to areas in Yunan Province along the border with Lao PDR and Myanmar (Wozencraft et al. 2008, B.P.L. Chan, in litt. 2020). In a review of recent felid camera-trapping across 28 protected areas and 10 provinces / autonomous regions across China (939 camera-trap stations and 283,239 trap-nights) between 2007 and 2019 Mainland Clouded Leopard were detected in three sites: Medog County, Tibet Autonomous Region and two of four protected areas (Yiwu and Tongbiguan) in Yunnan Province (Liu et al. 2020). In a review of recent range-wide records Petersen et al. (2020a) found published records of Mainland Clouded Leopard from only one (Medog County) of 25 camera-trapping studies in the species’ predicted range. More recent camera-trapping from the Chinese Felid Conservation Alliance appear to have detected Mainland Clouded Leopard from a number of additional sites in Yunnan province, thus a more thorough assessment of the status of the species in China is required (A. Giordano in litt. 2020).

Thailand
Mainland Clouded Leopards appear to be widely distributed throughout Thailand’s highly fragmented forests based on the results of a recent literature review (Petersen et al. 2020a). As is common elsewhere across the species range, most records in Thailand are derived from tiger survey bycatch data; therefore, generalizations about possible occurrence in unsurveyed areas should be made cautiously. Recent published camera-trap records (2010 onwards) confirm the presence of at least one individual in most major forest complexes (i.e., WEFCOM, Kaeng Krachan FC, Khlong Saeng-Khao Sok FC, Hala Bala FC, Eastern FC, Dong-Phayayen-Khao Yai FC, and Phu Khieo-Nam Nao FC). The species status in less frequently surveyed areas, however, is uncertain. Specifically, there are a lack of recent published records from the relatively unexplored forest complexes in northern (i.e., Lum Nam Pai-Salawin FC, Sri Lanna-Khun Tan FC, Doi Phu Kha-Mae Yom FC, Mae Ping-Om Koi FC, and Phu Meang-Phu Thong FC), northeastern (i.e., Phu Parn FC and Phanom Dongkrak-Pha Tam), and southern Thailand (i.e., Khao Luang FC and Khao Bantad FC).

Cambodia
Mainland Clouded Leopard historically occurred throughout Cambodia’s evergreen and semi-evergreen forests and was likely only absent from the lowlands surrounding the Tonle Sap. However, the species has declined significantly in both distribution and abundance in the past 20 years with post 2014 records from only Siem Pang Wildlife Sanctuary and Virachey National Park in the northeast, and the Cardamom Rainforest Landscape in the southwest. The latter two sites (Virachey and the Cardamoms) represent the largest and most inaccessible evergreen forest landscapes in the country. Mainland Clouded Leopard have been recently (post-2018) recorded from camera-traps in multiple locations in Virachey National Park (McCann et al. 2020) and at least four protected areas in the Cardamom Rainforest Landscape (Botum Sakor National Park, Central Cardamom National Park, Southern Cardamom National Park, and Tatai Wildlife Sanctuary (Gray et al. 2017). These two landscapes represent the last strongholds for Mainland Clouded Leopard in Cambodia, although in all sites the number of camera-trap records were insufficient to estimate density. Elsewhere in Cambodia Mainland Clouded Leopard have become extremely scarce and may be extirpated. In the Siem Pang Wildlife Sanctuary complex, Stung Treng Province, a single Mainland Clouded Leopard was photographed by camera-traps in April 2016 and a pregnant female was captured alive in a snare in February 2020 (J. C. Eames in litt. 2020). In the Eastern Plains Landscape, Mondulkiri Province, Mainland Clouded Leopard was last camera-trapped in December 2012 (from Phnom Prich Wildlife Sanctuary), with no documented records from the more extensive evergreen forests of Seima Wildlife Sanctuary since 2006 (when an individual was released alive from a snare) whereas the last camera-trap record was obtained from March 2003 (WWF-Cambodia, in litt. 2020). In the Northern Plains Landscape of Preah Vihear, the species was last detected on camera-traps from Chepp Wildlife Sanctuary in 2014 however one Mainland Clouded Leopard was camera-trapped from Phnom Dongrak, on the border with Thailand, in November 2020 (L. Grassman, in litt., 2020). There are no recent records from Prey Long Wildlife Sanctuary (WCS-Cambodia, in litt. 2020). In the adjacent Phnom Tnaout Wildlife Sanctuary apparent Mainland Clouded Leopard tracks were recorded in 2014 but have not been found subsequently (S. Davis, in litt. 2020).

Viet Nam
Mainland Clouded Leopard was historically widespread throughout the evergreen forests of Viet Nam however there are no recent records and the species is likely close to extinction from the country due to industrial levels of snaring and other hunting. The last documented record of Mainland Clouded Leopard from Viet Nam was from Pu Luong (a protected area dominated by karst limestone forests and thus protected, to some extent, from snaring) in December 2003. In their country-wide review of the status of wild cats, Wilcox et al. (2014) documented only two other (earlier) confirmed records of Mainland Clouded Leopard across the country between 1995 and 2013. Whilst there is possibility of dispersal into remote areas of Viet Nam from Lao PDR (A. Giordano in litt., 2020) camera-trap studies since 2013 across the country from at least 19 protected areas, including Pu Luong, have not detected the species.

MalaysiaMainland Clouded Leopards are still relatively widespread across Peninsular Malaysia (Perhiltan 2017), and can be found all the way from the north of the country bordering Thailand, to the most southern state of Johor. They predominantly occur within the Central Forest Spine map (DTCP 2009), a ~51,000 km² landscape which forms the majority of Peninsular Malaysia’s remaining forests, which includes large protected-area complexes (e.g., Belum-Temengor, Taman Negara, Endau Rompin), as well as Forest Reserves (e.g., Pasoh FR, Ulu Muda FR, Pasir Raja Selatan FR, Tanum FR, Sungai Yun FR), and Linkage areas (Primary Linkage 7, Primary Linkage 8, Tan et al. 2017, Rostro-García et al. unpub. data). Much of it is contiguous, and the areas outside it are relatively small and fragmented – even if they still harbor Mainland Clouded Leopards they might not persist over the long-term.
documentation.population:
The continued expansion of camera-trapping (including a number of studies targeted on Mainland Clouded Leopard) across the species’ range means that we have a better understanding of Mainland Clouded Leopard population and densities than in the previous assessment in 2016. At least six studies have published density estimates for Mainland Clouded Leopards with estimates varying between 0.3 individuals per 100 km² (across large areas of Southern Bhutan: Penjor et al.2018) to 5.14 individuals per 100 km² Dampa Tiger Reserve, India (Singh and MacDonald 2017). However, in the majority of locations across the species’ range there are too few camera-trap detections to estimate density and in other, apparently suitable sites (see Geographic Range) there have been no recent records. Camera-trap detection rates and naïve /modelled camera-trap occupancy vary extensively across the species’ range. This variation is likely linked to both sampling design and ecological conditions (e.g. lower intrinsic carrying capacity for Mainland Clouded Leopard in high elevation areas in the northern and western extremes of the range; Can et al. 2020) and anthropogenic pressures particularly poaching. In their range-wide camera-trap analysis MacDonald et al. (2019) reported naïve occupancy (from the 39 of 45 studies which detected the species) of between 0.02 and 0.44.

In Peninsular Malaysia, documented declines in tiger abundance during the assessment period (WWF Tigers Alive Initiative, in litt. 2020) and evidence of targeted poaching of large cats, particularly using cable snares, suggests Mainland Clouded Leopard populations will have declined in the past 21 years. On at least two recent occasions (in 2017 and 2018) organized Vietnamese poaching gangs in Malaysia have been apprehended with body parts of at least two Mainland Clouded Leopards, as well as tiger, bear and wild boar body parts (TRAFFIC 2019). Forested landscapes supporting Mainland Clouded Leopard in Malaysia receive less targeted protection than in some other range countries (e.g. Thailand, Nepal, India) and all occupied habitat is under, at least some, poaching pressure. In Manas Tiger Reserve in India the encounter rate of Mainland Clouded Leopard from camera-trapping has declined in recent years (J. Borah, in litt. 2020) though the extent to which this is due to behavioural changes following tiger recovery is unclear. In Thailand there are recent records from at least 14 protected areas in seven forest complexes (Petersen et al. 2020a) but evidence that densities are lower in more accessible and heavily hunted areas (Petersen et al. 2020b).

Camera-trap density estimates of Mainland Clouded Leopard exclude cubs (e.g. Petersen et al.2020b) thus we assume that published density estimates refer to mature individuals. Extrapolating published densities across the 558,000 km² of ‘good quality’ Mainland Clouded Leopard habitat modelled by MacDonald et al. (2019) would give a global population of between 1,600 and 29,000 adult individuals. Though a number of the areas identified as high-quality habitat in this paper (e.g. in parts of Viet Nam and Lao PDR) are unlikely to support the species due to hunting and habitat loss (Petersen et al.2020a). Nevertheless, the global Mainland Clouded Leopard population is probably incorporated within these bounds (e.g. 1,600–29,000) but is likely much more towards the lower end (see also Assessment Rationale) with range-wide average densities of ~1.0 individual per 100 km² more realistic. This would give a population of between ~5,580 (based on MacDonald et al. 2019 available habitat) and ~3,700 (based on Petersen et al. 2020a available habitat) mature individuals. Given continued habitat loss, fragmentation, and hunting across the range the population is inferred to be continuing to decline. Long-term monitoring of Mainland Clouded Leopard abundance within sites are recommended in order to more accurately observe or estimate rates of population change and this, potentially, trigger criterion C1 (i.e. <10,000 mature individuals and observed, estimated, or projected decline of >10% in three generations) in future assessments.
documentation.habitats:
The Mainland Clouded Leopard is intermediate in size between large and small cats, with wild females from Thailand weighing 11.5 (Austin and Tewes 1999) to 13.5 kg (Grassman et al. 2005), and males 16 (Grassman et al. 2005) to 18 kg (Austin and Tewes 1999). Its coat is patterned with distinctive large cloud shaped markings, its canines are exceptionally elongated, as is its tail - for a large cat (Sunquist and Sunquist 2002). The Mainland Clouded Leopard is highly arboreal and strongly associated with forest habitat, particularly primary evergreen tropical rainforest, but there are also records from dry and deciduous forest, as well as secondary and logged forests. They have been recorded in the Himalayas at elevations above 3,500 m (Can et al. 2020, Y. Ghimrey in litt., 2020).

Less frequently, they have been found in grassland and scrub, dry tropical forests and mangrove swamps (Nowell and Jackson 1996). Radio-tracking studies in Thailand have shown a preference for forest over more open habitats (Austin et al. 2007, Grassman et al. 2005). There is some evidence from Peninsular Malaysia for the ability of animals to persist amidst an agricultural matrix of certain land uses, including rubber (Mukri et al. unpub.; A. Giordinao in litt., 2020).

A study in Thailand's Phu Khieo Wildlife Sanctuary found that Mainland Clouded Leopards preyed upon a variety of arboreal and terrestrial prey, including hog deer, slow loris, brush-tailed porcupine, Malayan pangolin and Indochinese ground squirrel (Grassman et al. 2005). Other observations include mainly primate prey, but also muntjac and Argus pheasant (Nowell and Jackson 1996). Mainland Clouded Leopards are primarily nocturnal, with crepuscular activity peaks (Grassman et al. 2005, Austin et al. 2007).

Two radio-telemetry studies in different parks in Thailand found that adult male and female Mainland Clouded Leopards had similar home range sizes between 30-40 km² (95% fixed kernel estimators), with smaller intensively used core areas of 3-5 km² (Grassman et al. 2005, Austin et al. 2007). While both studies found substantial home range overlap between males and females, as is typical of most felids, Grassman et al. (2005) also found that the ranges of their two radio-collared males overlapped by a significant amount (39%). Although both studies found similar home ranges, Mainland Clouded Leopards in Phu Khieo Wildlife Sanctuary travelled approximately twice the average daily distance (average 2 km) than Mainland Clouded Leopards in Khao Yai National Park (Grassman et al. 2005, Austin et al. 2007).

Mainland Clouded Leopards may occur at higher densities when densities of the larger cats, tigers and leopards, are lower (Lynam et al. 2001, Grassman et al. 2005, Petersen et al. 2020b).
documentation.threats:
Mainland Clouded Leopards prefer closed forest (Grassman et al. 2005, Austin et al. 2007), and their habitat in Southeast Asia is undergoing amongst the world's fastest deforestation rates (0.6% per year between 1990 and 2010; Stibig et al. 2014). A recent modelling paper estimated a range-wide decline in the area of habitat categorised as strongholds for Mainland Clouded Leopard (defined as large contiguous areas of high-quality habitat where the species could survive over the mid-to-long term) of 34% between 2000 and 2018 (Petersen et al. 2020a). In addition to direct habitat loss the degradation of habitat and loss of functional connectivity is likely impacting many Mainland Clouded Leopard populations and, with future infrastructure development, particularly in Myanmar, this is likely to become a significant issue (Kaszta et al. 2020). A boom in large number of hydropower projects and rural roads in Mainland Clouded Leopard habitat is also a potentially significant threat in Nepal (Ghimirey and Acharya 2018).

Nevertheless, the biggest drive of population decline in Mainland Clouded Leopard during the assessment period was likely mortality due to illegal hunting – both targeted hunting for trade and incidental capture in indiscriminate hunting snares. The low number of detections or absence of the species from areas of suitable habitat particularly within Myanmar and Indochina indicates the scale of this threat. For example, in Cambodia the most recent records of the species from two apparently suitable sites (Western Seam Pang and Keo Seima Wildlife Sanctuaries) were of individuals captured in ungulate hunting snares. The rapid spread of snaring across Lao PDR and Cambodia, during the assessment period (and in Viet Nam largely prior to the current assessment) is likely the biggest cause of population decline during this period.

The Mainland Clouded Leopard is also hunted for the illegal wildlife trade. Large numbers of skins have been seen in market surveys, and there is also trade in bones for medicines to supplement the tiger bone trade, meat for exotic dishes and live animals for the pet trade (Hunter 2011). Wild animals are likely to be the primary source, but there is also some illegal trade from captive animals (Nowell 2007). For more details of trade driven threats see Use and Trade above.

Additional possible threats to Mainland Clouded Leopard which may require further research and analysis include prey depletion. This is potentially a threat in Indochina and China but seems likely to be a less significant issue elsewhere in the range. Can et al. (2020) also highlighted the potential impact of climate change on Mainland Clouded Leopard particularly on higher elevation populations in central Nepal.
documentation.measures:
Included on CITES Appendix I and protected by national legislation over most of its range (Nowell and Jackson 1996). However, in all countries, particularly in Southeast Asia, the interpretation of the law protecting Mainland Clouded Leopard is imperfect and can be undermined by corruption. Fines and punishments also need to be increased.

Despite co-occurring with tiger in many protected areas, and the growth of camera-trapping studies, there are no published temporal trends in Mainland Clouded Leopard population size or density. This remains a research priority and such information would strengthen future assessments and implementation of conservation activities.

The species occurs in many protected areas, although direct exploitation, range fragmentation, and reduction in habitat quality have caused Mainland Clouded Leopard declines within protected areas across its range. Improving the effectiveness of Protected Area management through implementing the Zero Poaching tool-kit (http://zeropoaching.org/) and achieving Conservation Assured Tiger Standards (CA|TS; Pasha et al. 2018) is likely to significantly reduce threats impacting Mainland Clouded Leopard populations within protected areas.

Given that much Mainland Clouded Leopard occurs in transboundary conservation landscapes the species should be considered in transboundary conservation planning (Farhadinia et al. 2019).
documentation.use_trade: Mainland Clouded Leopard exploitation for pelts is well documented in several countries, and the species’ parts remain noted in trade. Whilst some market surveys are recording fewer Mainland Clouded Leopard items since ~2010 this may represent trade moving underground and becoming more difficult to detect particularly in notorious borders markets in Myanmar. Population declines and local extinctions may also be contributing to declines in the number of Mainland Clouded Leopard occurring in trade. Recent (2016/17) surveys in Mong La, Special Region 4, Shan State, Myanmar found 11 Mainland Clouded Leopard skulls and 4 full skins (Sapai Min, in litt. 2020) compared to 54 skulls in December 2013 and 17 skulls and 5 full skins in February 2009 (Nijman and Shepherd 2015). In contrast, at Tachilik, Shan State on the Myanmar-Thailand border 2016/17 surveys found 8 full skins and 17 Mainland Clouded Leopard skulls (Sapai Min, in litt. 2020) compared to 22 skulls and 4 full skins in February 2006 (Nijman and Shepherd 2015). Mainland Clouded Leopard trade is also reported in other range states with a seizure of 19 Mainland Clouded Leopard skins in Phnom Penh, Cambodia in October 2014 (S. Gauntlett, in litt. 2020). A recent study in Nepal found a total of at least 51 individual Mainland Clouded Leopards in trade in just over 30 years (Ghimirey and Acharya 2018) whilst in Northeast India six cases of Mainland Clouded Leopard seizures were reported between 2015 and 2020; five were of skin and one of teeth and bones (J. Borah, in litt. 2020) and three cases of illegal poaching of Mainland Clouded Leopard were recorded from Bhutan in 2013/14 (W. M. Wong, in litt. 2020). These seizures and surveys likely represent a small proportion of the trade in Mainland Clouded Leopard parts in Asia, and highlight that wild off-take (either targeted poaching or through capture in indiscriminate hunting methods such as snares) is likely causing declines in many populations.
documentation.rationale:
Mainland Clouded Leopard populations continue to decline in the majority of range countries with the species being less abundant and with a reduced distribution than when last assessed in 2016. A decline in both range and abundance of >30% over the last three generations (generation length = 7 years [Pacifici et al. 2013] x 3 = 21 years, 1999–2019) is inferred due to a combination of direct exploitation and targeted hunting, incidental mortality due to snares set for other species (however any Mainland Clouded Leopard caught would likely enter trade), and habitat loss. A recent study estimated a range-wide decline in the area of habitat categorised as strongholds (defined as large contiguous areas of habitat identified as high-quality from species distribution models where the species could survive over the mid-to-long term) of 34% between 2000 and 2018 (Petersen et al. 2020a). Given that Mainland Clouded Leopard populations are impacted by both hunting and habitat loss, it is likely that actual population declines due to a combination of habitat loss and overhunting may exceed this.

In assessing the range-wide decline in Mainland Clouded Leopard since 1999, we assume that 60% of the 1999 population occurred in Bangladesh, Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar, China, and Viet Nam, and that across these countries the species’ population has declined by at least 45% over the past 21 years (1.9% decline per year). We assume 15% of the 1999 population was in Malaysia and that this has experienced a 20% decline since 1999 (0.9% per year) and 25% of the 1999 population was in Thailand, India, Nepal, and Bhutan with a 10% decline (0.5% per year). The assumptions above, in terms of percentage declines and percentage of the 1999 population within different countries, were inferred based on the expert opinion of the assessors. Overall, this results in a 32.5% decline in abundance from 1999-2019 (3 generations) and an IUCN Listing as Vulnerable under Criteria A2cd. As these threats are viewed as unlikely to cease, and in some cases may not be reversible, future declines are also suspected. Given the lower proportion of the 2019 population occurring in countries facing significant future declines (e.g. Indochina, Myanmar) a future reduction of mature individuals >30% seems less likely and thus Criteria A3 is not triggered. However, this situation may change if illegal wildlife trade expands to other countries currently not as affected. Mainland Clouded Leopard does qualify for Vulnerable under Criteria A4cd i.e. considering a 21-year time period including both the past and future (e.g. 2010–2031).

Mainland Clouded Leopard parts remain noted in trade with seizures and trade survey records indicating that wild off-take (either targeted poaching or through capture in indiscriminate hunting methods such as snares) is likely causing declines in many populations. As a result of hunting mortality and habitat loss, it is likely that Mainland Clouded Leopard populations have declined by much more than 30% during 1999–2019 (three generations) in at least Myanmar, Cambodia, Lao PDR, Viet Nam, Bangladesh, and China. Populations of Mainland Clouded Leopard at the beginning of 1999 were likely relatively large, and a significant contribution to the global population, in Myanmar, Cambodia, and Lao PDR. As such, declines in these countries are likely to have made a strong contribution to range-wide declines. Whilst populations in Viet Nam and China (see Geographic Range) also declined significantly during the assessment period, the 1999 population in these countries was likely comparatively small, and thus they would have made a less important contribution to overall population decline. Declines in these six countries are driven by a combination of targeted poaching for large cats (particularly in Myanmar), habitat loss, and incidental capture in snares (particularly in Indochina). Snaring has been implicated in declines of many ground-dwelling forest dependent species throughout Cambodia, Lao PDR, and Viet Nam (Belecky and Gray 2020) including big cats (Rasphone et al. 2019, Rostro-García et al. 2016) and is likely to have impacted Mainland Clouded Leopard populations in all three countries. In Cambodia and Lao PDR, the intensification of snaring throughout forests and protected areas occurred during the assessment period. For example, between 2010 and 2019 more than 195,000 snares were removed by law enforcement patrol teams from Cambodia’s Cardamom Rainforest Landscape (Belecky and Gray 2020)– an area which likely supports one of a few remaining large Mainland Clouded Leopard populations in Indochina.

Trends in Mainland Clouded Leopard populations in the other range countries (Nepal, Bhutan, India, Malaysia, and Thailand) are less clear. In Nepal, Bhutan, and India the species largely occurs in relatively well managed protected areas which are fairly secured from habitat loss and protected, to a degree, from poaching. In Malaysia and Thailand, Mainland Clouded Leopard populations likely face threats intermediate between those in Indochina and the Indian sub-continent with intermediate levels of poaching and habitat loss. However, there have been no published studies looking at changes in Mainland Clouded Leopard density or abundance over time from anywhere in the species’ range (which includes a number of high-profile Tiger Reserves and Tiger Protected Areas).

Estimating the global population of Mainland Clouded Leopard is difficult with little consistent range-wide data however it is highly likely that there are fewer than 10,000 mature individuals. Published density estimates for the species, from protected areas in the Indian Subcontinent, northern Myanmar, Malaysia, and Thailand, vary between 0.3 and 5.14 mature individuals per 100 km² (Borah et al. 2014, Petersen et al. 2020b). There are no published density estimates from Cambodia, China, Lao PDR, or Viet Nam. However, in many sites in which the species has been detected (often as by-catch from camera-trap efforts focusing on tigers) there are insufficient detections to estimate density suggesting densities may be lower than those reported in the literature. The range-wide models of MacDonald et al.(2019) estimated approximately 558,000 km2 of high-quality Mainland Clouded Leopard habitat across the species’ range (Macdonald et al. 2019) which was revised to ~370,000 km² using more recent forest cover data (Petersen et al.2020a). An average density between ~1.8 and 2.7 individuals per 100 km² across all high-quality habitat (dependent on the year of forest cover estimation) would be required for a global population of >10,000 mature individuals. Given likely absence due to hunting (See Geographic Range / Population / Threats) in some of these areas, and the low camera-trap detection rates in many other places, this range-wide density estimate seems too high. As such this assessment believes that the likely Mainland Clouded Leopard population is <10,000 mature individuals. However, estimated, as opposed to inferred, rates of population decline are required to trigger Vulnerable under criterion C1. Long-term monitoring of Mainland Clouded Leopard abundance within sites are recommended in order to more accurately observe or estimate rates of population change and this, potentially, trigger criterion C1 in future assessments.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Classically considered a single species, the Clouded Leopard has been split into two species. Based on analysis of mitochondrial DNA, microsatellites and morphology, Neofelis nebulosa is restricted to mainland Southeast Asia, and N. diardi is found on the islands of Sumatra and Borneo (Buckley-Beason et al. 2006, Kitchener et al. 2006, Wilting et al. 2007). The subspecific classification of Neofelis nebulosa needs further analyses (Kitchener et al. 2017). In addition to the nominate form two subspecies of Mainland Clouded Leopard have been described: N. n. macrosceloides (Hodgson in Gray, 1853, pl. 38) from Nepal, Northeast India, and Bhutan and (the presumably extinct) N. n. brachyura (Swinhoe, 1862, 352, pl. 43) from Taiwan. However, the recent review of wild cat taxonomy felt there was insufficient evidence for these two subspecies and proposed to keep N. nebulosa as monotypic until there was further evidence for subspecification (Kitchener et al. 2017).
